title: Pour un statut sémiologique du personnage
annotation: A foundational structural-semiotic account of character as a sign-system within narrative. Hamon relates a character’s identity to textual designation, description, action, recurrence, and relations with other signs.
citation_chicago_author_date: Hamon, Philippe. 1972. “Pour un statut sémiologique du personnage.” *Littérature* 6 (2): 86–110. https://doi.org/10.3406/litt.1972.1957.

title: Story and Discourse: Narrative Structure in Fiction and Film
annotation: A general theory of narrative in verbal and visual media. Its distinction between story-level existents (including characters) and discourse-level presentation remains a useful cross-media foundation.
publication_note: First published in 1978; later paperback and electronic editions are not separate records.
citation_chicago_author_date: Chatman, Seymour. 1978. *Story and Discourse: Narrative Structure in Fiction and Film*. Cornell University Press.

title: Characterization in Narrative: Some Theoretical Prolegomena
annotation: A compact theoretical account of how narrative texts characterize agents and how readers infer properties from words, actions, and narrative structure.
citation_chicago_author_date: Margolin, Uri. 1983. “Characterization in Narrative: Some Theoretical Prolegomena.” *Neophilologus* 67: 1–14. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01956983.

title: The Doer and the Deed: Action as the Basis for Characterization in Narrative
annotation: Argues that action and the relation between an agent and deeds are central to characterization. Useful for models that derive traits, motives, and identity from narrative conduct.
citation_chicago_author_date: Margolin, Uri. 1986. “The Doer and the Deed: Action as the Basis for Characterization in Narrative.” *Poetics Today* 7 (2): 205–225. https://doi.org/10.2307/1772759.

title: Introducing and Sustaining Characters in Literary Narrative: A Set of Conditions
annotation: Sets out conditions under which a character is introduced, tracked, and sustained as an identifiable narrative individual. No article-level DOI or stable article URL was located; the link is to the journal archive.
citation_chicago_author_date: Margolin, Uri. 1987. “Introducing and Sustaining Characters in Literary Narrative: A Set of Conditions.” *Style* 21 (1): 107–124.

title: Structuralist Approaches to Character in Narrative: The State of the Art
annotation: A state-of-the-field survey that maps structuralist theories of character and distinguishes approaches to role, textual construction, reference, and narrative individuality.
citation_chicago_author_date: Margolin, Uri. 1989. “Structuralist Approaches to Character in Narrative: The State of the Art.” *Semiotica* 75 (1–2): 1–24. https://doi.org/10.1515/semi.1989.75.1-2.1.

title: The What, the When, and the How of Being a Character in Literary Narrative
annotation: Examines what counts as a character, when a character exists in a narrative world, and how character identity is constituted. The cited issue/archive record is stable; no article-level DOI was found.
citation_chicago_author_date: Margolin, Uri. 1990. “The What, the When, and the How of Being a Character in Literary Narrative.” *Style* 24 (3): 453–468.

title: Individuals in Narrative Worlds: An Ontological Perspective
annotation: Develops an ontological account of individuals in narrative worlds, clarifying how fictional characters can be referred to, individuated, and related to the worlds in which they appear.
citation_chicago_author_date: Margolin, Uri. 1990. “Individuals in Narrative Worlds: An Ontological Perspective.” *Poetics Today* 11 (4): 843–871. https://doi.org/10.2307/1773080.

title: The Construction of Literary Character: A View from Cognitive Psychology
annotation: Introduces cognitive-psychological explanations of how readers build and update representations of literary characters from textual cues and prior knowledge. The page range follows the journal issue, not a later miscitation.
citation_chicago_author_date: Gerrig, Richard J., and David M. Allbritton. 1990. “The Construction of Literary Character: A View from Cognitive Psychology.” *Style* 24 (3): 380–391.

title: Narrative Fiction: Contemporary Poetics
annotation: An influential introduction to narrative poetics, including a systematic account of characterization, character types, presentation, and the relation between character and narration.
publication_note: Second edition (2002) selected; first edition appeared in 1983. The Routledge DOI points to the second edition.
citation_chicago_author_date: Rimmon-Kenan, Shlomith. 2002. *Narrative Fiction: Contemporary Poetics*. 2nd ed. Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203426111.

title: Figur und Person: Beitrag zu einer historischen Narratologie
annotation: A historical narratology of character and personhood, tracing how literary figures are made intelligible through historically situated concepts of person, individual, and social type.
citation_chicago_author_date: Jannidis, Fotis. 2004. *Figur und Person: Beitrag zu einer historischen Narratologie*. De Gruyter. https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110201697.

title: The One vs. the Many: Minor Characters and the Space of the Protagonist in the Novel
annotation: Analyzes how novels distribute narrative space and attention among protagonists and minor characters, linking characterization to social structure, plot, and unequal representational space.
citation_chicago_author_date: Woloch, Alex. 2003. *The One vs. the Many: Minor Characters and the Space of the Protagonist in the Novel*. Princeton University Press. https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctt7srp4.

title: Grundriß zur kognitiven Theorie der Figurenrezeption am Beispiel des viktorianischen Romans
annotation: A book-length cognitive model of how readers process characters, developed through Victorian fiction. It links textual cues, readers’ knowledge, inference, categorization, and emotional response.
citation_chicago_author_date: Schneider, Ralf. 2000. *Grundriß zur kognitiven Theorie der Figurenrezeption am Beispiel des viktorianischen Romans*. Stauffenburg.

title: Toward a Cognitive Theory of Literary Character: The Dynamics of Mental-Model Construction
annotation: Models character reception as a dynamic interaction between textual information and reader knowledge. Mental representations are elaborated, revised, categorized, or personalized as reading proceeds.
citation_chicago_author_date: Schneider, Ralf. 2001. “Toward a Cognitive Theory of Literary Character: The Dynamics of Mental-Model Construction.” *Style* 35 (4): 607–640. https://doi.org/10.5325/style.35.4.607.

title: The Cognitive Theory of Character Reception: An Updated Proposal
annotation: Revisits and updates Schneider’s cognitive account of character reception, emphasizing how textual representation interacts with readers’ cognitive and emotional activity.
citation_chicago_author_date: Schneider, Ralf. 2013. “The Cognitive Theory of Character Reception: An Updated Proposal.” *Anglistik* 24 (2): 117–134.

title: On the Twofoldness of Character
annotation: Reassesses the twofold character of fictional figures as both person-like entities and constructed representations, clarifying implications for theory and reader response.
citation_chicago_author_date: Smith, Murray. 2011. “On the Twofoldness of Character.” *New Literary History* 42 (2): 277–294. https://doi.org/10.1353/nlh.2011.0022.

title: Characters in Film and Other Media: Theory, Analysis, Interpretation
annotation: A comprehensive multidimensional framework for analyzing characters as represented beings, artifacts, symbols, and symptoms. The open-access book is designed for theory, close analysis, and interpretation across media.
publication_note: English translation/revision of Eder’s *Die Figur im Film* (2008; revised German edition 2014), counted as one 2025 English-language work. Publisher lists 228 pages; RWTH metadata lists 211.
citation_chicago_author_date: Eder, Jens. 2025. *Characters in Film and Other Media: Theory, Analysis, Interpretation*. Translated by Stephen Lowry in collaboration with Jens Eder. Open Book Publishers. https://doi.org/10.11647/OBP.0283.

title: Characters in Fictional Worlds: Understanding Imaginary Beings in Literature, Film, and Other Media
annotation: A major interdisciplinary collection spanning character ontology, representation, characterization, reception, identity, and transmediality. Distinct chapters are separately catalogued where they make citable contributions.
publication_note: Cited as 2010, the print/ebook copyright-publication year; some De Gruyter citation exports display 2011. The volume is one edited-book record, not separate format records.
citation_chicago_author_date: Eder, Jens, Fotis Jannidis, and Ralf Schneider, eds. 2010. *Characters in Fictional Worlds: Understanding Imaginary Beings in Literature, Film, and Other Media*. De Gruyter. https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110232424.

title: Characters in Fictional Worlds: An Introduction
container_title: Characters in Fictional Worlds: Understanding Imaginary Beings in Literature, Film, and Other Media
annotation: The editors synthesize major questions and methods in character analysis, including ontology, characterization, reader response, cultural meaning, and characters across media.
publication_note: The publisher’s chapter record gives pp. 3–66; some bibliographies shorten this to pp. 3–64. The catalogue follows the publisher pagination and the 2010 volume date.
citation_chicago_author_date: Eder, Jens, Fotis Jannidis, and Ralf Schneider. 2010. “Characters in Fictional Worlds: An Introduction.” In *Characters in Fictional Worlds: Understanding Imaginary Beings in Literature, Film, and Other Media*, edited by Jens Eder, Fotis Jannidis, and Ralf Schneider, 3–66. De Gruyter. https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110232424.1.3.

title: The Rhetoric of Fiction
annotation: A foundational rhetorical theory of fiction that informs the study of character as a vehicle for values, judgment, and readerly engagement, complementing structuralist and cognitive models.
publication_note: Second edition (1983) selected; the original appeared in 1961. Later editions are not separate records.
citation_chicago_author_date: Booth, Wayne C. 1983. *The Rhetoric of Fiction*. 2nd ed. University of Chicago Press. https://doi.org/10.7208/chicago/9780226065595.001.0001.

title: The Ontology of Fictional Characters
container_title: Characters in Fictional Worlds: Understanding Imaginary Beings in Literature, Film, and Other Media
annotation: A philosophical account of what fictional characters are and how apparently true claims about them can be understood. A useful counterpoint to semiotic, cognitive, and reception-oriented theories.
publication_note: Chapter year follows the volume’s 2010 publication date; some De Gruyter exports show 2011.
citation_chicago_author_date: Reicher, Maria E. 2010. “The Ontology of Fictional Characters.” In *Characters in Fictional Worlds: Understanding Imaginary Beings in Literature, Film, and Other Media*, edited by Jens Eder, Fotis Jannidis, and Ralf Schneider, 111–133. De Gruyter. https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110232424.2.111.

title: Character and Person
annotation: An interdisciplinary theory of character as an ontologically ambivalent construct and quasi-person. Frow links fictional figures to culturally and historically shaped models of social personhood.
citation_chicago_author_date: Frow, John. 2014. *Character and Person*. Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780198704515.001.0001.

title: L’effet-personnage dans le roman
annotation: A French narratological account of the ‘character effect’: how textual strategies and readers’ expectations produce the experience of a character in the novel.
publication_note: Second edition (1998) of a work first published in 1992; formats and reprints are not separate records.
citation_chicago_author_date: Jouve, Vincent. 1998. *L’effet-personnage dans le roman*. 2nd ed. Presses Universitaires de France. https://doi.org/10.3917/puf.jouve.1998.01.

title: Fictional Minds
annotation: Develops a theory of fictional minds that treats readers’ understanding of novels as tracking individual and interrelated character consciousnesses. Important for social minds and multi-character narrative engagement.
citation_chicago_author_date: Palmer, Alan. 2004. *Fictional Minds*. University of Nebraska Press.

title: Character: Three Inquiries in Literary Studies
annotation: Three complementary inquiries reopen character-based criticism: Moi on character as person-like, Felski on identification, and Anderson on thinking with characters and their moral lives.
citation_chicago_author_date: Anderson, Amanda, Rita Felski, and Toril Moi. 2019. *Character: Three Inquiries in Literary Studies*. University of Chicago Press. https://doi.org/10.7208/chicago/9780226658834.001.0001.

title: Engaging Characters: Fiction, Emotion, and the Cinema
annotation: A revised cognitive theory of spectators’ engagement with film characters, including recognition, alignment, and allegiance. Its concepts also influence literary and game-character research.
publication_note: Revised second edition published in 2022; first edition appeared in 1995. One record for the revised work, not one per format or edition.
citation_chicago_author_date: Smith, Murray. 2022. *Engaging Characters: Fiction, Emotion, and the Cinema*. 2nd rev. ed. Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780198871071.001.0001.

title: Activity Types and Characterisation in Dramatic Discourse
container_title: Characters in Fictional Worlds: Understanding Imaginary Beings in Literature, Film, and Other Media
annotation: Uses activity types and pragmatic expectations to explain how dramatic dialogue builds character and generates effects such as humor, incongruity, and irony.
publication_note: A separately authored chapter in the 2010 Eder et al. volume; the year follows the volume’s original publication date.
citation_chicago_author_date: Culpeper, Jonathan, and Dan McIntyre. 2010. “Activity Types and Characterisation in Dramatic Discourse.” In *Characters in Fictional Worlds: Understanding Imaginary Beings in Literature, Film, and Other Media*, edited by Jens Eder, Fotis Jannidis, and Ralf Schneider, 176–207. De Gruyter. https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110232424.3.176.

title: Reading People, Reading Plots: Character, Progression, and the Interpretation of Narrative
annotation: Introduces a rhetorical model of character’s mimetic, thematic, and synthetic functions and relates character development to narrative progression and readerly interpretation.
citation_chicago_author_date: Phelan, James. 1989. *Reading People, Reading Plots: Character, Progression, and the Interpretation of Narrative*. University of Chicago Press.

title: The Art of Sympathy in Fiction: Forms of Ethical and Emotional Persuasion
annotation: Combines narratology, aesthetics, psychology, and empirical literary study to explain how narratives invite sympathy for characters, including morally difficult or unsympathetic figures.
citation_chicago_author_date: Sklar, Howard. 2013. *The Art of Sympathy in Fiction: Forms of Ethical and Emotional Persuasion*. John Benjamins. https://doi.org/10.1075/lal.15.

title: Pour une analyse de l’effet-personnage
annotation: A concise French narratological proposal for analyzing the ‘character effect’: the textual and readerly processes through which a character is apprehended and experienced. It complements Jouve’s book-length study of the same concept.
publication_note: Distinct from T23, *L’effet-personnage dans le roman* (1992; cited here in its 1998 second edition), and T33, *La poétique du roman* (1997). The 1998 date is an edition of the 1992 book, not a separate work.
citation_chicago_author_date: Jouve, Vincent. 1992. “Pour une analyse de l’effet-personnage.” *Littérature* 85 (1): 103–111. https://doi.org/10.3406/litt.1992.2607.

title: Character
annotation: A concise handbook overview of character as a narratological category, its historical theories, ontological questions, and methods of characterization and analysis.
citation_chicago_author_date: Jannidis, Fotis. 2014. “Character.” In *Handbook of Narratology*, vol. 1, 2nd ed., edited by Peter Hühn, Jan Christoph Meister, John Pier, and Wolf Schmid, 30–45. De Gruyter. https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110316469.30.

title: Character Constellations in Cognitive and Empirical Literary Studies: A New Approach to Readerly Engagement
annotation: Develops an integrative model of readers’ engagement with constellations of characters, joining cognitive and empirical literary studies with classical literary scholarship.
publication_note: Fixed as T32 and counted as one monograph regardless of hardback, paperback, or ebook. Routledge lists 228 pages; the RWTH record lists 211.
citation_chicago_author_date: Schneider, Ralf. 2026. *Character Constellations in Cognitive and Empirical Literary Studies: A New Approach to Readerly Engagement*. Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003589365.

title: La poétique du roman
annotation: A French-language poetics of the novel, offering a broader account of novelistic form and reading than Jouve’s separate study of the character effect.
publication_note: A distinct title first published in 1997; it is not an edition or alternate title of *L’effet-personnage dans le roman*.
citation_chicago_author_date: Jouve, Vincent. 1997. *La poétique du roman*. SEDES.

title: Language and Characterisation: People in Plays and Other Texts
annotation: A book-length linguistic and cognitive account of how language creates impressions of people in plays and other texts, with extensive use of Shakespeare and cross-genre examples.
citation_chicago_author_date: Culpeper, Jonathan. 2001. *Language and Characterisation: People in Plays and Other Texts*. Longman.

title: Transmedial Narratology and Contemporary Media Culture
annotation: A major transmedial narratology that compares narrative representation in contemporary film, comics, and video games, including the representation of character subjectivity.
publication_note: First published 2016; the 2018 paperback is a reprint and is not a separate record.
citation_chicago_author_date: Thon, Jan-Noël. 2016. *Transmedial Narratology and Contemporary Media Culture*. University of Nebraska Press. https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctt1d8h8vn.

title: Toward a Typology of Transmedia Characters
annotation: Proposes a preliminary typology for how characters are constructed and transformed across media, addressing continuity, identity, and the semiotic status of transmedia figures.
citation_chicago_author_date: Bertetti, Paolo. 2014. “Toward a Typology of Transmedia Characters.” *International Journal of Communication* 8: 2344–2361.

title: Transtextual Characters
container_title: Characters in Fictional Worlds: Understanding Imaginary Beings in Literature, Film, and Other Media
annotation: Examines how characters persist and change across multiple texts and what criteria support claims of identity. Transtextual recurrence is broader than cross-media franchising.
publication_note: A separately authored chapter in the 2010 Eder et al. volume; cited under the volume’s original publication year.
citation_chicago_author_date: Richardson, Brian. 2010. “Transtextual Characters.” In *Characters in Fictional Worlds: Understanding Imaginary Beings in Literature, Film, and Other Media*, edited by Jens Eder, Fotis Jannidis, and Ralf Schneider, 527–541. De Gruyter. https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110232424.6.527.

title: Transmedia Characters: Theory and Analysis
annotation: Builds a method that begins with local, work-specific characters and then examines their relations within broader transmedia character networks through redundancy, expansion, or modification.
citation_chicago_author_date: Thon, Jan-Noël. 2019. “Transmedia Characters: Theory and Analysis.” *Frontiers of Narrative Studies* 5 (2): 176–199. https://doi.org/10.1515/fns-2019-0012.

title: Introduction: Characters across Media
annotation: Introduces a special issue on characters across media and frames the conceptual and methodological problems involved in tracing characters through convergent media cultures.
citation_chicago_author_date: Thon, Jan-Noël, and Lukas R. A. Wilde. 2019. “Introduction: Characters across Media.” *Frontiers of Narrative Studies* 5 (2): 169–175. https://doi.org/10.1515/fns-2019-0011.

title: Transmedia Characters: Additionality and Cohesion in Transfictional Heroes
container_title: The Routledge Companion to Transmedia Studies
annotation: Uses Sherlock Holmes, Batman, and Star Trek to analyze how producers add material to character-based transfictions and how audiences judge cohesion across versions.
publication_note: Chapter first published with the companion in 2018; its core argument revises Pearson’s 2017 article. The 2017 precursor is not counted as a second record.
citation_chicago_author_date: Pearson, Roberta. 2018. “Transmedia Characters: Additionality and Cohesion in Transfictional Heroes.” In *The Routledge Companion to Transmedia Studies*, edited by Matthew Freeman and Renira Rampazzo Gambarato, 148–156. Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781351054904-17.

title: Buck Rogers in the 25th Century: Transmedia Extensions of a Pulp Hero
annotation: Traces the evolution of Buck Rogers across media and applies a character-analysis model to a historically extended pulp-fiction franchise.
citation_chicago_author_date: Bertetti, Paolo. 2019. “Buck Rogers in the 25th Century: Transmedia Extensions of a Pulp Hero.” *Frontiers of Narrative Studies* 5 (2): 200–219. https://doi.org/10.1515/fns-2019-0013.

title: Transmedia Characters
annotation: A paired scholarly exchange that sharpens distinctions between transmedia characters and transmedia figures and discusses how characters are understood across media versions.
citation_chicago_author_date: Thon, Jan-Noël, and Roberta Pearson. 2022. “Transmedia Characters.” *Narrative* 30 (2): 139–151. https://doi.org/10.1353/nar.2022.0007.

title: Towards a Semiotic Theory of Transmedia Characters
annotation: Develops a semiotic account of characters across media, connecting textual character construction with intertextual, cultural, and social processes of recognition.
citation_chicago_author_date: Bertetti, Paolo, and Mattia Thibault. 2022. “Towards a Semiotic Theory of Transmedia Characters.” *Narrative* 30 (2): 225–239. https://doi.org/10.1353/nar.2022.0013.

title: Transmedia Character Studies
annotation: A comprehensive methodological toolkit for studying characters across multimodal, interactive, narrative, and non-narrative media, integrating production, texts, and reception.
citation_chicago_author_date: Kunz, Tobias, and Lukas R. A. Wilde. 2023. *Transmedia Character Studies*. Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003298793.

title: Video Game Characters and Transmedia Storytelling: The Dynamic Game Character
annotation: Introduces the dynamic game character, whose identity can vary with player choices, and examines tensions between player agency, transmedia continuity, and Euro-American and Japanese character traditions.
publication_note: First published open access by Amsterdam University Press in 2023; later Routledge-branded ebook and format records are not separate entries.
citation_chicago_author_date: Blom, Joleen. 2023. *Video Game Characters and Transmedia Storytelling: The Dynamic Game Character*. Amsterdam University Press. https://doi.org/10.5117/9789463722957.

title: Arthur/Artoria/Arthas. Some Theoretical Remarks on Arthur(ian) Characters in Contemporary Media Culture
annotation: Uses Arthurian figures, including Artoria and Arthas, to distinguish work-specific characters, transtextual characters, transmedia characters, and broader transmedia figures across media and cultures.
citation_chicago_author_date: Thon, Jan-Noël. 2025. “Arthur/Artoria/Arthas. Some Theoretical Remarks on Arthur(ian) Characters in Contemporary Media Culture.” *Journal of Literary Theory* 19 (2): 404–435. https://doi.org/10.1515/jlt-2025-2019.

title: Introduction: Graphic Narrative
annotation: A field-shaping introduction to graphic narrative that foregrounds the verbal, visual, and spatial resources through which comics represent people and structure readers’ interpretation.
citation_chicago_author_date: Chute, Hillary L., and Marianne DeKoven. 2006. “Introduction: Graphic Narrative.” *MFS Modern Fiction Studies* 52 (4): 767–782. https://doi.org/10.1353/mfs.2007.0002.

title: Comics and Narration
annotation: Extends Groensteen’s comics theory to narration and character subjectivity; chapter six analyzes how comics provide access to characters’ inner lives through visual and verbal means.
publication_note: English translation of the 2011 French *Bande dessinée et narration*; counted once as the 2013 English-language edition.
citation_chicago_author_date: Groensteen, Thierry. 2013. *Comics and Narration*. Translated by Ann Miller. University Press of Mississippi. https://doi.org/10.14325/mississippi/9781617037702.001.0001.

title: Characters in Comic Books
container_title: Characters in Fictional Worlds: Understanding Imaginary Beings in Literature, Film, and Other Media
annotation: A medium-specific examination of comic-book characters and the representational devices and cultural conventions through which they are constructed.
publication_note: Cited as 2010, matching the volume’s original print/ebook publication; some publisher citation exports use 2011.
citation_chicago_author_date: Aldama, Frederik Luis. 2010. “Characters in Comic Books.” In *Characters in Fictional Worlds: Understanding Imaginary Beings in Literature, Film, and Other Media*, edited by Jens Eder, Fotis Jannidis, and Ralf Schneider, 318–328. De Gruyter. https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110232424.3.318.

title: Contemporary Comics Storytelling
annotation: Applies cognitive narratology to contemporary comics, including a case study of fictional minds, characterization, and ethics in *100 Bullets*.
citation_chicago_author_date: Kukkonen, Karin. 2013. *Contemporary Comics Storytelling*. University of Nebraska Press. https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctt1ddr8c6.

title: The Visual Language of Comics: Introduction to the Structure and Cognition of Sequential Images
annotation: Proposes a cognitive-linguistic account of comics as a structured visual language. Relevant to how character appearance, action, and relations become legible across sequential images.
publication_note: The work appeared online in 2013; paperback listings may carry a 2014 date.
citation_chicago_author_date: Cohn, Neil. 2013. *The Visual Language of Comics: Introduction to the Structure and Cognition of Sequential Images*. Bloomsbury Academic. https://doi.org/10.5040/9781472542175.

title: On the Level: A Dramaturgical Approach to the Comics Character
container_title: Journal of Graphic Novels and Comics
annotation: Adapts Earle Gister’s dramaturgical concepts into a framework for analyzing comics characters as stock figures, realist characters, stereotypes, or political actors.
publication_note: Online first in 2023; cited under the 2024 version-of-record issue year.
citation_chicago_author_date: Anthony, Trevor F. 2024. “On the Level: A Dramaturgical Approach to the Comics Character.” *Journal of Graphic Novels and Comics* 15 (1): 49–65. https://doi.org/10.1080/21504857.2023.2220392.

title: Character-Driven Game Design: A Design Approach and Its Foundations in Character Engagement
publisher: Aalto University School of Arts, Design and Architecture
annotation: Proposes a character-driven design method connecting character traits, social conflict, gameplay rules, and player experience; developed alongside the game *Lies and Seductions*.
publication_note: Article-based doctoral thesis. Its included papers are not counted as extra records solely because they appear in the dissertation.
citation_chicago_author_date: Lankoski, Petri. 2010. *Character-Driven Game Design: A Design Approach and Its Foundations in Character Engagement*. Doctoral dissertation, Aalto University School of Arts, Design and Architecture.

title: Player Character Engagement in Computer Games
annotation: Adapts film theory’s recognition, alignment, and allegiance to explain empathic and goal-related engagement with player characters.
publication_note: The separately published 2011 journal article also appears in the 2010 article-based dissertation (T53); it is retained as an independently citable journal publication, not as a format duplicate.
citation_chicago_author_date: Lankoski, Petri. 2011. “Player Character Engagement in Computer Games.” *Games and Culture* 6 (4): 291–311. https://doi.org/10.1177/1555412010391088.

title: Video Game Characters. Theory and Analysis
container_title: DIEGESIS: Interdisciplinary E-Journal for Narrative Research
annotation: A foundational integrative model distinguishes narration, simulation, and communication; narrative, ludic, and social experience; and characters as fictional beings, game pieces, or representations of players.
citation_chicago_author_date: Schröter, Felix, and Jan-Noël Thon. 2014. “Video Game Characters. Theory and Analysis.” *DIEGESIS: Interdisciplinary E-Journal for Narrative Research* 3 (1): 40–77. https://www.diegesis.uni-wuppertal.de/index.php/diegesis/article/view/151.

title: The Ludic Subject and the Ludic Self: Analyzing the ‘I-in-the-Gameworld’
annotation: A major phenomenological account of the player’s ‘I’ within the gameworld, clarifying how playable figures, character identity, agency, and experience relate.
citation_chicago_author_date: Vella, Daniel. 2015. *The Ludic Subject and the Ludic Self: Analyzing the ‘I-in-the-Gameworld’*. PhD diss., IT University of Copenhagen.

title: My Avatar and Me: Toward a Cognitive Theory of Video Game Characters
container_title: Video Games and the Mind: Essays on Cognition, Affect, and Emotion
annotation: Develops a cognitive framework for experiencing and analyzing video-game characters, integrating narrative representation with gameplay, bodily response, and player-character interaction.
citation_chicago_author_date: Schröter, Felix. 2016. “My Avatar and Me: Toward a Cognitive Theory of Video Game Characters.” In *Video Games and the Mind: Essays on Cognition, Affect, and Emotion*, edited by Bernard Perron and Felix Schröter, 32–52. McFarland.

title: Better Game Characters by Design: A Psychological Approach
annotation: A research-informed professional guide translating social psychology and interpersonal perception into practical principles for designing game characters and interactions.
publication_note: Classified as design practice informed by psychology, not as peer-reviewed research.
citation_chicago_author_date: Isbister, Katherine. 2006. *Better Game Characters by Design: A Psychological Approach*. Morgan Kaufmann.

title: Playing with Character: A Framework of Characterization in Video Games
annotation: Synthesizes literary, film, and game studies into a framework for game characterization, including developer, actor, and player contributions and player effort as ‘ergodic characterization.’
publication_note: First published online in 2023; cited under the 2024 version-of-record issue year.
citation_chicago_author_date: Vandewalle, Alexander, Steven Malliet, and Kristoffel Demoen. 2024. “Playing with Character: A Framework of Characterization in Video Games.” *Games and Culture* 19 (6): 722–742. https://doi.org/10.1177/15554120231179496.

title: Character Creation Processes in Video Games
annotation: A recent reference overview of player-facing game character creation, linking appearance, identity cues, functional choices, self-representation, and motivation.
publication_note: Living reference work entry first published online 7 July 2026; classified as an academic reference entry rather than an empirical study.
citation_chicago_author_date: Türkay, Selen. 2026. “Character Creation Processes in Video Games.” In *The Palgrave Encyclopedia of Cyberpsychology*, edited by Chris Fullwood, Dawn Branley-Bell, Lisa J. Orchard, Maria Limniou, and Vasilena Stefanova, 1–5. Palgrave Macmillan. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-52643-5_3-1.

title: The Art of Dramatic Writing: Its Basis in the Creative Interpretation of Human Motives
annotation: A highly influential craft manual that treats character motivation, contradiction, and conflict as engines of dramatic action. Included as a practitioner source, not an academic study.
publication_note: The Art of Dramatic Writing title was published in 1946; later revised/reprint editions are not separate records. Egri’s earlier *How to Write a Play* (1942) is not separately counted.
citation_chicago_author_date: Egri, Lajos. 1946. *The Art of Dramatic Writing: Its Basis in the Creative Interpretation of Human Motives*. Simon and Schuster.

title: A Short Organum for the Theatre
container_title: Brecht on Theatre: The Development of an Aesthetic
annotation: Brecht’s influential practitioner-theory essay on theatrical representation and acting. Its approach helps contextualize character as performed, socially legible, and open to critical distance.
publication_note: English translation in the 1964 Willett anthology; the German essay was written in 1948 and first published in 1949. One translated essay record, not separate anthology/translation formats.
citation_chicago_author_date: Brecht, Bertolt. 1964. “A Short Organum for the Theatre.” In *Brecht on Theatre: The Development of an Aesthetic*, edited and translated by John Willett, 179–205. Hill and Wang.

title: Impro: Improvisation and the Theatre
annotation: A practitioner’s account of improvisation, status, spontaneity, masks, and narrative skills, relevant to generating characters through embodied play and interaction.
publication_note: First published in 1979; later Methuen/Routledge reprints are not counted separately.
citation_chicago_author_date: Johnstone, Keith. 1979. *Impro: Improvisation and the Theatre*. Faber and Faber.

title: The Actor and the Target
annotation: A practical acting method that redirects attention from internal self-consciousness toward the ‘target’ beyond the actor, offering a usable framework for embodied character work.
publication_note: The English edition first appeared in 2002; this record cites the revised and updated 2005 edition as one work.
citation_chicago_author_date: Donnellan, Declan. 2005. *The Actor and the Target*. Revised ed. Nick Hern Books.

title: Into the Woods: A Five Act Journey into Story
annotation: A screenwriting and story-structure guide from a British television executive and writer. Useful for the interaction of character desire, opposition, transformation, and act structure.
publication_note: First UK ebook/hardback publication in 2013; a Penguin paperback edition followed in 2014. The paperback is not a separate record.
citation_chicago_author_date: Yorke, John. 2013. *Into the Woods: A Five Act Journey into Story*. Particular Books.

title: The Science of Writing Characters: Using Psychology to Create Compelling Fictional Characters
annotation: A writer-facing handbook that translates personality psychology, including the Big Five, into exercises and tools for building characters, dialogue, motivation, relationships, and change.
publication_note: First published in 2020; later ebook and print manifestations are one work. Classified as research-informed practice, not peer-reviewed research.
citation_chicago_author_date: Pelican, Kira-Anne. 2020. *The Science of Writing Characters: Using Psychology to Create Compelling Fictional Characters*. Bloomsbury Academic. https://doi.org/10.5040/9781501357213.

title: Building Character: An Analysis of Character Creation
annotation: A veteran game designer’s industry guide to building player-facing characters, covering backstory, observable traits, appearance, motivation, and design choices.
publication_note: Originally published on Gamasutra; migrated to Game Developer. This is an industry-practice article, not an academic study.
citation_chicago_author_date: Meretzky, Steve. 2001. “Building Character: An Analysis of Character Creation.” *Game Developer*, November 19, 2001.

title: The Writing of The Witcher 3
annotation: Interview with lead writer Jakub Szamałek on iterative dialogue, character and story documents, open-world narrative, and the production constraints behind the Polish studio’s game.
publication_note: Industry reporting/interview; not peer-reviewed research. A direct page request was blocked during verification, but date, author, title, and content were verified from search-indexed publication data.
citation_chicago_author_date: Stuart, Keith. 2019. “The Writing of The Witcher 3.” *Eurogamer*, October 15, 2019.

title: The Making of Disco Elysium: How ZA/UM Created One of the Most Original RPGs of the Decade
annotation: Reports on the Estonian ZA/UM collective’s route from tabletop worldbuilding and fiction to a dense, reactive RPG, with attention to writing systems and character psychology.
publication_note: Trade journalism based on developer interviews; useful as production testimony, not as peer-reviewed evidence.
citation_chicago_author_date: Wiltshire, Alex. 2020. “The Making of Disco Elysium: How ZA/UM Created One of the Most Original RPGs of the Decade.” *GamesRadar+*, January 9, 2020.

title: Q&A with Writer Sally Abbott
annotation: A BBC Writers Q&A in which British television writer Sally Abbott describes developing credible characters, contrasting their traits, tracking needs and secrets, writing a voice, and learning from continuing-drama production.
publication_note: Creator interview/resource rather than academic research.
citation_chicago_author_date: BBC Writers. 2015. “Q&A with Writer Sally Abbott.” September 14, 2015.

title: 10 Screenwriting Tips from Maren Ade
annotation: A filmmaker’s account of character-led writing, especially entering each character’s perspective, attending to personal needs, and using research, rehearsal, and editing as part of script development.
publication_note: Creator-interview material selected for its direct account of the German writer-director’s process; not a scholarly source. Originally published 17 October 2016; the BFI page was updated 7 April 2017.
citation_chicago_author_date: Stevens, Isabel. 2016. “10 Screenwriting Tips from Maren Ade.” *Sight and Sound* (BFI), October 17, 2016.
